title: Seni's Law: Mental Health Units (Use of Force) Act 2018
blurb: Know what counts as force, the duties on every mental health unit, and what you must record after using force.
question: During a night shift on an acute ward, staff hold Kemi's arms for 4 minutes to prevent her hitting another patient, then give IM lorazepam. A healthcare assistant asks whether any of this needs recording under 'Seni's Law'. What should the nurse explain?

teach.body: The Mental Health Units (Use of Force) Act 2018 is known as Seni's Law, after Olaseni (Seni) Lewis, a young Black man who died following the disproportionate use of force in a mental health unit; his family campaigned for change. The Act makes the use of force in mental health units transparent and accountable and aims to reduce it. In plain English: every unit must have someone in charge of reducing force, tell patients their rights, train staff and record each use of force.
teach.cite: Mental Health Units (Use of Force) Act 2018; DHSC statutory guidance, 7 Dec 2021

head: Type
Definition in the Act
rows: Physical contact intended to prevent, restrict or subdue movement
A device restricting movement, mainly for behavioural control
Medication intended to prevent, restrict or subdue movement
Any seclusion or segregation imposed on a patient
teach.caption: Applies to NHS mental health units in England and independent hospitals providing NHS-funded mental health care.

steps.label: Responsible person
steps.sub: One senior employee for all units (s2)

steps.label: Policy
steps.sub: Written policy on use of force (s3)

steps.label: Patient information
steps.sub: Rights about force, soon after admission (s4)

teach.h: What the record must include (s6(5), examples)
head: About
Items recorded
rows: Reason; place, date and duration; type(s) of force; how force was used
Patient's name and identifier; staff names and job titles
Mental disorder; relevant characteristics; learning disability or autism
Efforts made to avoid force; whether it was in the care plan
Outcome; whether care-plan notifications were sent
teach.caption: Records are kept for 3 years (s6(6)). Negligible force need not be recorded (s6(2)), as defined in the statutory guidance.

items.label: Core duties in force (ss1-6 and others)

teach.caption: Statutory guidance for NHS organisations and police was published on 7 December 2021.

teach.h: Training content the Act lists (s5(2), selection)
items: Involving patients in planning their care, and respecting their past and present wishes and feelings.
Respecting diversity and avoiding unlawful discrimination, harassment and victimisation.
Techniques for avoiding or reducing the use of force, and the risks of force.
The impact of trauma and of any use of force on mental and physical health and development.

teach.body: When a police officer goes into a mental health unit on duty to assist staff, they must wear and operate a body camera at all times when reasonably practicable (s12). This adds transparency to some of the highest-risk restraint situations. Staff remain responsible for patient care, including monitoring airway, breathing and vital signs during and after any restraint.

Holding Kemi's arms to stop her moving is physical restraint; IM lorazepam given to subdue her is chemical restraint. Both are uses of force that must be recorded, with the reason, duration, types of force, staff involved, efforts to de-escalate first, whether it was in her care plan and the outcome. The nurse completes the record, monitors Kemi after rapid tranquillisation, offers a debrief and checks she has the unit's information on her rights about force.

teach.text: 'Use of force' is wider than hands-on restraint: it includes chemical restraint (medication to subdue) and isolation (seclusion or segregation). Only NEGLIGIBLE force, as defined in the statutory guidance, is exempt from recording.

items: Use of force = physical, mechanical or chemical restraint, or isolation.
Each organisation: one senior responsible person, a policy, patient information, staff training with refreshers.
Record every non-negligible use of force, including efforts to avoid it; keep records for 3 years.
Police assisting in a unit wear body cameras when reasonably practicable; core duties in force since 31 March 2022.

summary: You can now define use of force under Seni's Law, describe the duties on every mental health unit and record a use of force correctly. You know when the Act came into force and what police officers must do when assisting in a unit.

A.q: Under the Mental Health Units (Use of Force) Act 2018, which of these is a 'use of force'?
options: Offering oral medication the patient accepts
Asking a patient to return to their room
A.why: Section 1(6): use of force includes the isolation of a patient, meaning any seclusion or segregation imposed on them.

whyNot.0: Accepted oral medication is not intended to subdue movement against the patient's will.
whyNot.2: A verbal request involves no restraint or isolation.
whyNot.3: Observation is not restraint or isolation.

A.q: How long must records of the use of force be kept under the Act?
A.why: Section 6(6): the responsible person must keep the record for 3 years from the date it was made.

whyNot.0: One year is shorter than the statutory period.
whyNot.1: Six months is shorter than the statutory period.
whyNot.3: Eight years is a common health records period, not the Act's requirement.

A.q: How many responsible persons must a trust that runs four mental health units appoint under the Act?
A.why: Section 2(3): an organisation operating more than one mental health unit must appoint a single responsible person for all of them.

whyNot.0: The Act does not require a responsible person per ward.
whyNot.2: A single responsible person covers all the organisation's units.
whyNot.3: The Act requires one responsible person; deputies may help but the duty is single.

B.q: Staff give a patient intramuscular medication to subdue her violent behaviour during an incident. How is this classed under the Act?
B.why: Section 1(7): chemical restraint means medication intended to prevent, restrict or subdue movement of the patient's body.

B.q: Police are called to help staff restrain a patient on an acute mental health ward. What does the Act require of the officers?
options: Wear and operate body cameras when practicable
Leave once the patient is on the floor
Complete the unit's own use of force record for it
Take the patient to a police station
B.why: Section 12: a police officer going into a mental health unit on duty to assist staff must wear and operate a body camera at all times when reasonably practicable.

whyNot.1: This is not a statutory requirement, and floor restraint should be avoided where possible.
whyNot.2: Recording under s6 is the unit's responsibility.
whyNot.3: The patient is already in hospital; removal to a police station is not required.

B.q: When must a patient be given the unit's information about their rights regarding use of force?
options: After the first time force is used on them on the ward
At their first tribunal hearing on detention
As soon as reasonably practicable after admission
On the day they are discharged from the unit
B.why: Section 4(4)(b): information must be provided as soon as reasonably practicable after the patient is admitted, and steps taken to help them understand it.

whyNot.0: Patients need the information before any force is used.
whyNot.1: The tribunal has no role in this duty.
whyNot.3: Information at discharge is too late to protect their rights.

C.q: After restraining Kemi, a nurse records the time, staff involved and the outcome. Which important item required by the Act is missing?
options: Efforts made to avoid using force
C.why: Section 6(5)(o): the record must include any efforts made to avoid the need to use force on the patient.

whyNot.0: The nearest relative's address is not a listed item.
whyNot.2: Budget information is not part of the record.
whyNot.3: GP details are not a listed item.

C.q: A new healthcare assistant starts on a mental health unit. Under section 5, when should they receive use-of-force training?
options: Within the first twelve months of their employment
After they are first involved in a restraint incident
As soon as reasonably practicable after starting
Before their first annual appraisal meeting
C.why: Section 5(3)(b): training must be provided as soon as reasonably practicable after a person becomes a member of staff, with refresher training at regular intervals.

whyNot.0: A year's delay is not 'as soon as reasonably practicable'.
whyNot.1: Training must come before staff are involved in incidents where possible.
whyNot.3: Appraisal timing is not the statutory test.

C.q: On which date did the core duties of the Mental Health Units (Use of Force) Act 2018, such as recording use of force, come into force?
C.why: SI 2021/1372 brought ss1-6 (other than s6(5)(n)), s9 (other than s9(e)), 10, 11, 13 and 15 into force on 31 March 2022.

whyNot.0: The Act was passed in November 2018 but its duties were commenced later.
whyNot.2: 18 August 2022 is when the s12 police body camera duty began.
whyNot.3: 6 April 2026 relates to commencement of parts of the Mental Health Act 2025.

reteach.title: P, P, I, T, R
reteach.question: What five things must every mental health unit have in place under Seni's Law?

blocks.body: A PERSON responsible (one senior employee for the organisation). A POLICY on reducing force. INFORMATION for patients about their rights. TRAINING for staff, refreshed regularly. RECORDS of every use of force that is not negligible, kept for 3 years. Police helping on the unit wear body cameras when practicable.

blocks.text: Rapid tranquillisation used to subdue a patient is chemical restraint and must be recorded as a use of force.

explain.body: Force means physical, mechanical or chemical restraint, or isolation (seclusion or segregation). The Act covers NHS mental health units in England and independent hospitals providing NHS-funded mental health care.

test.q: Long-term segregation of a patient counts under the Act as which type of force?
test.why: Section 1(7): isolation means any seclusion or segregation imposed on a patient.

explain.body: Each organisation appoints one responsible person, employed by it and of appropriate seniority, covering all its mental health units. They own the policy, information, training and records.

test.q: Which requirement applies to the responsible person under section 2?
options: They must be a consultant psychiatrist in the trust
They must be employed and suitably senior
They must be a police liaison officer
They must be independent of the trust
test.why: Section 2(2): the responsible person must be employed by the organisation and of an appropriate level of seniority.

whyNot.0: The Act does not specify a profession.
whyNot.2: Police have separate duties under s12.
whyNot.3: They must be employed by the organisation.

explain.body: Every use of force that is not negligible is recorded with set details, including reason, duration, types, staff, the patient's characteristics, efforts to avoid force and outcome. Kept for 3 years.

test.q: Which use of force does NOT need to be recorded under section 6?
options: Force included in the care plan
test.why: Section 6(2): the duty to record does not apply where the force is negligible, as defined in the statutory guidance.

whyNot.0: Short restraint is still recorded if not negligible.
whyNot.1: Force by any staff working in the unit is recorded.
whyNot.3: The record notes whether force was in the care plan; it is still recorded.

explain.body: Staff are trained soon after joining, with regular refreshers, covering de-escalation, trauma, risks of force, diversity and law. Patients receive information on their rights about force soon after admission.

test.q: Which topic must use-of-force training cover under section 5?
options: The impact of trauma on health
test.why: Section 5(2)(g): training must include the impact of trauma (historic or otherwise) on a patient's mental and physical health.

whyNot.1: Budgeting is not a listed topic.
whyNot.2: Prescribing is not a listed training topic.
whyNot.3: Tribunal reports are not a listed topic.
